video_title: How GTA VI Became the Most Expensive Video Game Ever Made | Odd Lots
gist: Bloomberg games reporter Jason Schreier explains how GTA VI became a roughly $1B+, 4,700-person, eight-year project that only Rockstar can justify because of GTA's franchise certainty and Take-Two's in-game-monetization model, with record preorders pointing to a possible doubling of GTA V's launch revenue. He argues GTA VI is an anomaly rather than an industry blueprint, as most publishers cut budgets, while AI data center demand for GPUs and memory is driving up PC and console hardware prices.

themes.theme: GTA VI launch scale and demand signals

insights.claim: Grand Theft Auto V (2013) has sold about 235 million copies, making it the best-selling non-mobile (console/PC) game of all time; only Minecraft, counting phones, sells more.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: The installed fan base behind GTA VI is unmatched, underpinning near-certain launch demand for Take-Two.

insights.claim: PlayStation and Xbox both said GTA VI broke their records for the most video game preorders on their digital storefronts, with estimates of more than 10 million preorder copies (Rockstar and Take-Two have not confirmed numbers).
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Record preorders de-risk Take-Two's launch quarter and support platform-holder digital revenue.
insights.quote: their estimates that it could be more than 10 million copies on preorder

insights.claim: GTA V made roughly $800 million on its first day and about $1 billion in its first three days in 2013, and Schreier would not be shocked if GTA VI doubled that on day one given fan fervor above GTA V's level.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Sets a bar for day-one revenue expectations: roughly $1.6B+ day one would match the 'double' scenario.
insights.quote: I wouldn't be shocked if this hit double that in its first day

insights.claim: GTA VI is projected to make more in its first week or so than the film The Odyssey has made in its entire box office, and the hosts frame it as likely to generate about $5 billion in revenue relatively quickly against a rumored $1-1.5 billion budget.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier / Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Shows gaming's top franchises now out-earn the biggest film releases; relevant to entertainment share-of-wallet comparisons.

insights.claim: Rockstar premiered GTA VI's half-hour gameplay reveal on Netflix, and it became the number one piece of content on the service that week, beating a new Robert De Niro film.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Signals cross-media marketing pull and that game IP can drive streaming engagement; watch for more Netflix-game tie-ins.
insights.quote: more people wanted to watch a commercial for Grand Theft Auto six than wanted to watch a new movie from Robert De Niro

insights.claim: Anecdotal evidence suggests many people, including non-gamers, are taking PTO for the GTA VI launch and buying PlayStations just to play it, though Schreier dismisses market-research claims of 'billions in lost productivity' as headline-chasing nonsense.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: GTA VI may pull console hardware demand forward into the holiday quarter; discount productivity-loss headlines.
insights.quote: I don't really buy that stuff because it kind of seems like nonsense

insights.claim: Other big releases, even annual Call of Duty, are struggling partly because consumers are saving their money for GTA VI, meaning the launch cannibalizes competitors' sales.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Expect weaker sales for competing titles near GTA VI's launch window; a negative for rival publishers' near-term numbers.
insights.quote: Even one of the biggest franchises in the world, Call of Duty, is having a hard time right now, in part because a lot of people are saving their money for grand Theft Auto

themes.theme: Take-Two's recurring-revenue model and the 13-year gap

insights.claim: About 80% of Take-Two's revenue comes from in-game monetization (microtransactions) rather than game sales.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Take-Two is effectively a live-services business; recurring in-game spend matters more than unit sales.
insights.quote: something like 80% of their revenue comes not from sales, but from in-game monetization

insights.claim: GTA Online, launched as GTA V's multiplayer mode, grew into an estimated $500 million-a-year business from players buying outfits, guns and other in-game items, which reduced Rockstar's incentive to rush a sequel and helps explain the 13-year wait for GTA VI.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: A successful live-service tail can lengthen release cycles; watch whether GTA VI gets an online component that repeats the long-tail model.
insights.quote: there's a little bit less incentive to hurry up on a sequel because you have this long tail of just never ending revenue

insights.claim: Take-Two also owns Firaxis (maker of Sid Meier's Civilization, which released a new game last year), alongside Rockstar.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Take-Two has a broader studio portfolio beyond GTA, though GTA dominates the economics.

themes.theme: Exploding AAA budgets and why GTA VI is an anomaly

insights.claim: Game development has shifted from 2-3 year cycles with roughly $20 million budgets and teams under 100 people in the 2000s to 7-8 year cycles with budgets in the hundreds of millions, and GTA VI possibly more than $1 billion.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Rising cost per title concentrates risk; publishers' margins depend on fewer, bigger bets.

insights.claim: Rockstar roughly doubled its headcount from about 2,400 employees at the end of Red Dead Redemption 2 to about 4,700 to build GTA VI.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Headcount scale is the main cost driver; watch whether Rockstar holds or trims staff post-launch.
insights.quote: GTA six is made by a team of 4700 people

insights.claim: You can only spend more than $1 billion on a game if you know you will make it back, and GTA VI is about as sure a thing as exists in the volatile games industry.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: GTA VI's budget is justified by franchise certainty, not a template for others.
insights.quote: I think you can only spend more than $1 billion on a game if you know you're going to make it back

insights.claim: Schreier views GTA VI as an anomaly rather than the industry's blueprint: most publishers are trying to cut budgets because sales have not risen in step with $500-600 million development costs, leaving AAA economics in an 'untenable position'.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Expect cost cuts, smaller-scope projects and restructuring across other AAA publishers rather than copycat mega-budgets.
insights.quote: sales have not risen in correlation with these budgets going way, way up. And so it's kind of reached an untenable position

insights.claim: Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick joked that Rockstar is like his son who was given an unlimited wedding budget and surpassed it, illustrating that Rockstar effectively operates with a blank check because GTA's franchise power guarantees payback.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier (relaying Strauss Zelnick)
insights.so_what: Signals limited cost discipline at Rockstar is tolerated by management; margin depends on GTA's outsized revenue.
insights.quote: I told him, you can have an unlimited budget for your wedding. And he surpassed it

insights.claim: New franchises still break out, e.g. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 from a ~30-person French studio sold close to 10 million copies and Elden Ring sold around 30 million and is getting an Alex Garland film, but publishers find it far harder to justify hundreds of millions to launch new IP.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Small-team hits show lean-budget upside; capital is shifting toward low-cost new IP and proven franchises rather than expensive new AAA bets.

insights.claim: Whether Rockstar's spending is a reusable technology investment is uncertain: COVID closures of motion-capture studios added delays, an expansion within a year or two seems easy to imagine, but a next game not taking another 7-8 years is harder to imagine, though a now-established 4,700-person team and pipelines could speed future work if Rockstar does not double again.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Do not assume faster Rockstar release cadence; expansions/online content are the likelier near-term monetization.

insights.claim: Games and public markets clash because game development blends art and software and is inherently unpredictable, while markets demand predictability, a tension Schreier documented between Blizzard's creatives and Activision Blizzard's Bobby Kotick.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Treat game release dates and guidance as soft; delays are structural, not exceptional.
insights.quote: games are so unpredictable and markets demand predictability

insights.claim: GTA VI was announced in late 2023 with a 2025 target that insiders likely knew was never real, then delayed to May 2026 and again to November, with delays driven by the game's density and some parts taking longer than planned.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Even top studios miss dates twice; haircut publisher release timing in models.
insights.quote: That was not a real date, that was never a real date

themes.theme: AI chip demand squeezing gaming hardware

insights.claim: AI data centers buying up GPUs, RAM and storage have doubled or even tripled high-end graphics card prices from a former $700-800 ceiling, often with no availability, pushing PC gaming out of reach for many.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: AI capex is crowding out consumer gaming hardware; a headwind for PC gaming demand and a tailwind for memory/GPU pricing.
insights.quote: these AI data centers are buying up all the GPUs and all the Ram and all the storage

insights.claim: For the first time, console prices have risen after launch: PlayStation 5 launched at $500 in 2020 and is now $650 for the base model, and PlayStation, Switch and Xbox have all raised prices due to AI-driven component scarcity, reversing the historical pattern of consoles getting cheaper over time (PS4 launched at $400 and fell).
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Rising hardware prices shrink the addressable installed base and could cap software sales growth.
insights.quote: PlayStation five launched at $500 in 2020 and is now $650 for the base line model

insights.claim: There is widespread fear in the games industry that next-generation consoles could cost more than $1,000, which would put them out of reach for most people; relief may only come if data center moratoriums persist and memory/GPU markets normalize.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Watch next-gen console pricing as a key risk to platform growth; data center moratoriums are a potential swing factor for memory/GPU supply.
insights.quote: the next iteration of consoles, could cost more than $1,000

insights.claim: The AI-chip-driven console shortage and price gouging could make it hard to buy a PlayStation alongside GTA VI at launch.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Hardware supply, not software demand, may be the binding constraint on GTA VI's launch reach.

insights.claim: GTA VI is digital only, about 210GB, too large for a disc; retail boxes contain only a download code, and PlayStation has announced it will phase out discs entirely starting in 2028.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Physical retail (e.g. game-disc sellers and resale) faces structural decline as distribution goes all-digital.
insights.quote: PlayStation has actually announced that they are phasing out discs entirely starting in 2028

insights.claim: Publishers favor digital because most of the market has already shifted to digital purchases, digital margins are significantly higher, huge file sizes don't fit on discs, and developers can work closer to the final deadline without manufacturing lead times.
insights.speaker: Jason Schreier
insights.so_what: Digital mix shift is margin-accretive for publishers and platform holders.
insights.quote: margins are significantly higher on digital sales
